content: Childhood body mass index (BMI) tracking revealed similar trends in both lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) and high-income countries (HICs). Thirteen studies demonstrated that elevated BMI during childhood or adolescence is associated with a higher risk of overweight or obesity in adulthood. Most studies predicted a significant risk of becoming overweight or obese based on weight status or rapid weight gain during infancy and childhood. Similar associations were observed with height status. Regarding hyperlipidemia, nine studies (eight cohort studies) examined the relationship between childhood anthropometric measures and total cholesterol levels in later life. Three studies found no association between childhood BMI and adult total cholesterol levels, while one study identified an inverse association in females only. Two studies reported a positive association between childhood BMI and adult total cholesterol, but one of these studies found no association after adjusting for adult BMI. Only one study showed a significant link between waist circumference at age 9 and increased total cholesterol levels between ages 12 and 14. Triceps skinfold thickness and the sum of skinfold thicknesses were positively correlated with adult total cholesterol levels. For triglycerides, 12 studies (10 cohort studies and one consortium) investigated the association between childhood anthropometric measures and triglyceride levels in adulthood. Eight studies reported a positive association between childhood BMI and adult triglyceride levels. One study found an inverse association, while another reported no association between childhood BMI and triglycerides measured during mid-childhood. Childhood weight status was positively associated with adult triglyceride levels, but height status showed no association. A rapid increase in waist circumference was positively linked to adult triglyceride levels. Eleven studies (six cohort studies and one consortium) explored the relationship between childhood and adolescent anthropometric measures and adult low-density lipoprotein (LDL) levels. Seven studies found that childhood and adolescent BMI were associated with adult LDL levels. One study reported a weak inverse association, while another linked childhood weight status to adult LDL levels. Additionally, one study found that the rate of height increase during childhood was associated with adult LDL levels. Two studies showed that a rapid increase in waist circumference was positively associated with adult LDL levels, and two studies found that childhood triceps skinfold thickness positively correlated with adult LDL levels. Fourteen studies (10 cohort studies and one consortium) examined the association between childhood and adolescent anthropometric measures and high-density lipoprotein (HDL) levels in adulthood. Most studies reported a negative association between childhood BMI and adult HDL levels. Weight status during childhood also showed a negative association in the majority of studies, while height status was not found to play a significant role. Two studies reported a negative association between childhood waist circumference and triceps skinfold thickness with adult HDL levels. Overweight and obesity are linked to numerous comorbidities, including cardiovascular disease (CVD), type 2 diabetes, and certain cancers. Over the past three decades, the prevalence of obesity and overweight has increased significantly in the pediatric population. This trend is observed globally, even in regions with high levels of maternal and child undernutrition. The rising prevalence of obesity represents a global public health issue, with an estimated 30% of coronary heart disease (CHD) and ischemic stroke and nearly 60% of hypertensive disease in developed countries attributable to excess BMI. Waist circumference may be a better predictor of CVD risk than BMI, but the independent effect of childhood obesity on adult cardiovascular health remains unclear. Adiposity has been shown to track from childhood into adulthood, potentially increasing the risk associated with adult obesity. From a public health perspective, it is crucial to determine whether childhood adiposity leads to adult adiposity, whether childhood overweight has adverse effects, or whether childhood adiposity increases cardiovascular risk. It is also important to assess whether anthropometric measures can predict later obesity, abnormal lipid profiles, subsequent cardiovascular disease, or type 2 diabetes mellitus. The aim of this review was to systematically and critically evaluate the available evidence regarding the predictive value of anthropometric measures in infants and children for developing cardiovascular disease or type 2 diabetes mellitus in later life. The review included prospective, retrospective cohort studies and longitudinal studies that examined anthropometric measures during infancy and childhood and their association with the risk of developing cardiovascular disease or type 2 diabetes mellitus in later life. Anthropometric measures evaluated included weight-for-age, height-for-age, weight-for-height, BMI, mid-upper arm circumference, skinfold thickness, adiposity, and waist circumference. Outcome measures included cardiovascular events (e.g., coronary artery disease, stroke) or type 2 diabetes mellitus. The review adhered to strict inclusion and exclusion criteria, ensuring the quality and relevance of the studies included. The literature search across multiple databases yielded 651 potentially relevant publications. After screening titles and abstracts, 167 references were identified as potentially relevant, with an additional 14 publications identified through reference checking. Approximately 40 cohort groups were identified, with evidence available from 31 studies conducted in high-income countries and nine studies from lowand middle-income countries. The review systematically assessed the predictive value of childhood anthropometric measures for later health outcomes, providing critical insights into the long-term impact of childhood obesity and related factors.
